note.text: A proposition asserts something. In standard categorical form, distinguish quantifier, subject term, copula and predicate term. Keep multiword terms intact. Parsing a claim does not verify its truth.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to separate quantifier, subject term, copula and predicate term in a standard categorical statement. Builds on: Form Three’s distinction between a term, a judgment and an argument. Leads to: categorical propositions, where these parts express a relation between classes.

sections.heading: A claim has a structure
sections.text: A proposition expresses an assertion that can be true or false. A question or command does not automatically assert a proposition. The standard categorical model makes its parts visible: quantifier + subject term + copula + predicate term. The quantifier sets the scope; the subject names the class discussed; the copula links; the predicate names the class attributed or denied. Other propositions need different analyses, which come later.

sections.heading: Follow the parts in a local example
sections.text: In an invented Buea club rule, All club members are badge holders, All is the quantifier, club members the subject term, are the copula and badge holders the predicate term. Both class expressions contain several words. A term is not restricted to one word, and naming the parts does not prove the club actually follows that rule.

sections.heading: Keep whole terms together
sections.text: First identify what class is discussed. Then locate the relation and the class attributed to it. Finally check the quantifier. In Some library books are not loanable items, library books is the subject, loanable items the predicate and are not the negative copula in this school model. The words not and are do not create a new class name.

key_words.meaning: how much of the subject class is covered
the class about which the claim is made
the linking expression joining subject and predicate
the class attributed to, or denied of, the subject

mistake.wrong: Each word is a separate logical term.
mistake.right: Club members is one multiword term.
mistake.why: Logical function depends on the expression’s role, not its word count.

worked_example.problem: Parse All library books are loanable items.
steps: Library books names the class discussed.
Are links that class to loanable items.
worked_example.answer: Quantifier: All; subject: library books; copula: are; predicate: loanable items.

cards.idea: Each part has a different job.
example: quantifier: All — how much of the subject class is covered.
subject term: club members — the class about which the claim is made.
copula: are — the linking expression joining subject and predicate.
predicate term: badge holders — the class attributed to, or denied of, the subject.

cards.idea: The subject is the whole class being discussed.
example: All library books are loanable items: library books is the subject.

cards.idea: A logical term can contain several words.
example: School gardens and cultivated areas each function as a term.

pick.q: In “All club members are badge holders,” which expression is one complete logical term?
e: All is the quantifier.
Are is the copula.
This combines separate functions and omits the class expression.
pick.y: A logical term may contain several words while naming one class.

wrong.text: Every individual word is a separate complete logical term.

wrong.text: The predicate is always the person speaking.
wrong.explain: The predicate term names the class attributed to or denied of the subject.

wrong.text: A question is a true-or-false assertion merely because it ends with a sign.
wrong.explain: A question asks for information; it does not by itself assert the requested claim.

wrong.text: Identifying sentence parts establishes the factual truth of a claim.
wrong.explain: Parsing establishes structure; checking the facts is a separate task.
